newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - UK pension funds seen subsidising tax cut.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - UK pension funds seen subsidising tax cut.

text.p: Some of Britain's top business leaders expect pension funds to be stripped of lucrative tax breaks if a Labour government is elected and implements plans to cut income tax for the lowest paid, a Reuters survey showed.

Of the 20 finance and managing directors of leading quoted companies who took part in the survey, 10 said they expected a reduction in advance corporation tax (ACT), which would hit tax-exempt organisations such as pension funds and individuals without tax liabilities.

Labour has pledged to keep standard and higher rates of income tax at current levels, and plans to implement a 10 percent band for the lower paid at a future date, giving rise to speculation that ACT would be a prime target to raise government revenue.
ACT, currently set at 20 percent, is levied from a company's gross profits at the same time as dividends are paid to shareholders.

It can be offset against a company's corporation tax liability, which means that although it does not increase a company's overall tax burden, it hastens the arrival of cash in government coffers by about nine months.

Tax-exempt organisations such as pension funds benefit from a higher rate of ACT because they can claim more cash back from the government, so they would bear the financial brunt of any Labour government's plans to drop the rate.
There is a precedent for increasing revenue by lowering ACT.
In 1993, then-Chancellor of the Exchequer Norman Lamont lowered the ACT rate to 20 percent from 25 percent, a move which raised an extra billion sterling in government revenue.
All 20 contributors to the survey said they expected Labour to win a majority over the ruling Conservative party on May 1.
The survey, which was carried out between March 25 and April 1, showed that 19 out of 20 contributors expect their companies to have a slightly heavier overall tax burden.
Labour currently has an enormous lead on the ruling Conservative party in public opinion polls and is heavily favoured to form the next British government after May 1 elections.
Thirteen of the finance directors in the poll said they expected more tax to be collected via higher corporation tax, currently levied at 33 percent.
But Lucy Chennells, senior research economist at the Institute of Fiscal Studies (IFS), said she did not expect any major changes in corporation tax.
"It's possible they'll raise it a little, but anything dramatic would probably wait until their second term," she said.
Analysts said they feared higher corporate tax receipts would be used to raise allowances on capital investment.
"The danger is they will encourage unnecessary investment which will ultimately lower growth, profitability and productivity," said Richard Jeffrey, group economist at Charterhouse.

Ten respondents in the poll said the Conservative government, traditionally perceived as the friend of big business, had been "quite good" for British business over the past five years and eight said they had been "very good" for business.
The survey showed that 17 out of 20 trusted the Conservative party most to represent British business interests.
Thirteen out of 15 companies expect interest rates to trend higher. The median of eight predictions from the survey shows base rates at seven percent by end-1997 and at eight percent by end-1999.

"I would agree interest rates will be around seven percent at end-1997, but I think your contributors are being pessimistic. I would expect rates to start falling, albeit in small steps, from mid-1998," a UK economist said.
